title: Valid Palindrome
description: Given a string, print 'true' if it reads the same forward and backward after converting all uppercase letters into lowercase letters and removing all non-alphanumeric characters. Print 'false' otherwise.
referenceSolution:
import sys

def solve():
    s = sys.stdin.read()
    filtered = [c.lower() for c in s if c.isalnum()]
    print("true" if filtered == filtered[::-1] else "false")

if __name__ == '__main__':
    solve()

title: Trapping Rain Water
description: Given n non-negative integers representing an elevation map where the width of each bar is 1, compute how much water it can trap after raining and print the total units.
referenceSolution:
import sys

def solve():
    s = sys.stdin.read().strip()
    if not s:
        print(0)
        return
    height = list(map(int, s.split()))
    if not height:
        print(0)
        return
    left, right = 0, len(height) - 1
    left_max, right_max = height[left], height[right]
    ans = 0
    while left < right:
        if left_max < right_max:
            left += 1
            left_max = max(left_max, height[left])
            ans += max(0, left_max - height[left])
        else:
            right -= 1
            right_max = max(right_max, height[right])
            ans += max(0, right_max - height[right])
    print(ans)

if __name__ == '__main__':
    solve()

title: Database Indexing & B-Trees
description: Explain how database indexing works, specifically focusing on B-Trees, logarithmic search time, and disk I/O reduction.
questionText: Explain how database indexing works, specifically focusing on B-Trees, logarithmic search time, and disk I/O reduction.
referenceAnswer: Database indexes use balanced B-Tree or B+ Tree data structures to organize indexed keys in sorted order. By storing multiple keys per node matching disk page block sizes, B-Trees maintain a very high branching factor and a shallow tree height. This guarantees O(log N) search, insertion, and deletion times while minimizing expensive disk I/O operations by reading entire index pages into memory cache in a single disk read.

title: ACID Transactions
description: Explain ACID properties in database management systems and how they ensure data integrity during concurrent transactions and system failures.
questionText: Explain ACID properties in database management systems and how they ensure data integrity during concurrent transactions and system failures.
referenceAnswer: ACID transactions guarantee reliable database operations through four core properties: Atomicity ensures that all operations in a transaction succeed completely or roll back entirely (all-or-nothing), typically managed via write-ahead logging (WAL). Consistency enforces that transactions transition the database only between valid states respecting all constraints and invariants. Isolation prevents concurrent transactions from interfering with each other using lock-based concurrency control or multi-version concurrency control (MVCC). Durability guarantees that committed modifications survive crashes through persistent storage flushes.

title: TCP vs UDP Protocols
description: Compare TCP and UDP protocols, detailing connection establishment, packet ordering, reliability, and typical use cases.
questionText: Compare TCP and UDP protocols, detailing connection establishment, packet ordering, reliability, and typical use cases.
referenceAnswer: TCP is a connection-oriented, reliable transport protocol that uses a three-way handshake (SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK) to establish a connection. It guarantees ordered packet delivery, error checking, and retransmission of lost packets through sequence numbers and acknowledgments, making it ideal for web browsing (HTTP), file transfers, and emails. In contrast, UDP is connectionless and lightweight without handshakes or delivery guarantees, minimizing latency and overhead. UDP is preferred for real-time applications such as video streaming, VoIP, and gaming where occasional packet loss is acceptable.

title: CAP Theorem in Distributed Systems
description: Explain Brewer's CAP Theorem, detailing the trade-offs between Consistency, Availability, and Partition Tolerance in distributed systems.
questionText: Explain Brewer's CAP Theorem, detailing the trade-offs between Consistency, Availability, and Partition Tolerance in distributed systems.
referenceAnswer: The CAP Theorem states that in a distributed data store, it is impossible to simultaneously guarantee more than two out of three guarantees: Consistency, Availability, and Partition Tolerance. Network partitions are unavoidable in real-world distributed infrastructure, meaning systems must choose between Consistency (CP) and Availability (AP) during a partition. CP systems reject inconsistent reads/writes to ensure linearizability, while AP systems continue serving all requests at the cost of eventual consistency and temporary stale reads.

title: JavaScript Event Loop
description: Explain the JavaScript Event Loop, distinguishing between the call stack, microtask queue (Promises), and macrotask queue (setTimeout).
questionText: Explain the JavaScript Event Loop, distinguishing between the call stack, microtask queue (Promises), and macrotask queue (setTimeout).
referenceAnswer: JavaScript is single-threaded and executes synchronous code on the call stack. When asynchronous operations occur, callbacks are deferred to task queues. The Event Loop continuously monitors the call stack: when the stack is empty, it first drains all jobs in the microtask queue (such as Promise callbacks, process.nextTick, MutationObserver) until empty, before taking the oldest task from the macrotask queue (such as setTimeout, setInterval, I/O events). This priority guarantees microtasks execute immediately after the current execution context completes.

title: Python Global Interpreter Lock (GIL)
description: Explain the Python Global Interpreter Lock (GIL), why it exists in CPython, and how it impacts CPU-bound vs I/O-bound multithreaded applications.
questionText: Explain the Python Global Interpreter Lock (GIL), why it exists in CPython, and how it impacts CPU-bound vs I/O-bound multithreaded applications.
referenceAnswer: The Global Interpreter Lock (GIL) is a mutex used by CPython to protect access to Python objects, preventing multiple native threads from executing Python bytecode simultaneously. The GIL simplifies CPython's memory management by avoiding race conditions in non-thread-safe reference counting. Consequently, CPU-bound multithreaded Python programs cannot achieve true multi-core parallelism and often experience performance degradation due to thread context switching contention. However, for I/O-bound tasks (such as network requests and file reads), threads release the GIL while waiting for I/O, allowing efficient concurrent execution.
